title: Kill switch or traffic switch
summary: Which probe restarts the container, which one only stops the traffic, and what each is safe to depend on. Pointing the kill switch at a shared dependency is how one database blip becomes a fleet-wide restart.

sources.author: Kubernetes
sources.title: Explore Termination Behavior for Pods And Their Endpoints

cards.front: Liveness and readiness both fail. One restarts the container and one does not. Which is which?
cards.back: Liveness failing restarts the container. Readiness failing removes the Pod's IP address from the EndpointSlices, so the traffic stops and the process keeps running.

cards.front: Your liveness probe queries the database. One blip later, why is every instance in the fleet restarting?
cards.back: Because liveness failing means kill, and every instance failed the same check in the same second. Dependencies belong in readiness, where failing means "not me" rather than "kill me".

cards.front: Readiness checks a dependency every instance shares, and it blips. What does the balancer have left to send to?
cards.back: Nothing: every endpoint is removed at once, and requests the cache could have served get a 503. Readiness is per instance, so check what this instance uniquely needs.

cards.front: On SIGTERM, why does failing readiness come before `server.close()` rather than after?
cards.back: Because whatever is in front of you learns on an interval, and closing first refuses connections it is still sending. nginx's passive check defaults to a `fail_timeout` of 10 seconds.

cards.front: Readiness answered 200 and the first few hundred requests still failed. What was it actually reporting?
cards.back: That the framework could answer, not that the process was ready: the endpoint said yes before the connection pool or cache warm-up existed. Start the flag at false and set it after boot.

cards.front: `server.close()` against `server.closeAllConnections()` in a shutdown. Which one belongs behind a deadline?
cards.back: `closeAllConnections()`, because it closes active connections too. `close()` stops new connections and never interrupts a request being served.

cards.front: The only thing hitting `/ready` is the platform. Why is it showing up in the database's load?
cards.back: Because probes are requests, one per instance per interval across the fleet. A readiness check that runs a real query on every probe is standing load on the database.
